_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- US Federal BACKWARD-COUNTED periods.
Phase 4 item 3.
WHY THIS EXISTS: the engine has supported backward counting since Phase 1 --
count.direction 'backward', a backward rollOff, and FRCP 6(a)(6)'s
direction-dependent state-holiday rule are all implemented and unit-tested --
but across Phases 1-3 not one of the sixteen seeded rules used it. All
sixteen were forward, calendar_days. That made backward counting the largest
gap between what the engine CAN do and what it had ever actually done on
real data, and backward trigger-date semantics are subtle enough that unit
tests alone are not proof.
EVERY VALUE READ FROM PRIMARY SOURCE 2026-08-22 AND QUOTED IN THE ROW.
WHY THE TRIGGER NAMES CARRY THE SUBJECT OF THE DEADLINE. Rule 26(a)(2)(D)(i)
and Rule 26(a)(3)(B) both run backward from the SAME calendar event -- the
date set for trial -- with different counts (90 and 30). Encoding both with a
single trigger_event would put two rules in force for one trigger, which the
engine correctly refuses as AMBIGUOUS_RULE, so neither would ever compute.
The distinguishing fact is WHICH disclosure is being made, which is a fact
about the question being asked rather than about the calendar. The trigger
name therefore carries it, exactly as Michigan's
service_of_summons_and_complaint_in_michigan carries a fact about how service
happened. The engine still never guesses between them; the caller states
which deadline they mean, and the UI shows each rule's own label and
citation so the choice is visible before a date is produced.
WHY BACKWARD ROLLOVER GOES BACKWARD, and why that direction is the only safe
one here. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(5), quoted: "The 'next day' is determined by
continuing to count forward when the period is measured after an event and
backward when measured before an event." So if the 90th day before trial is a
Sunday, the disclosure is due on the preceding FRIDAY, not the following
Monday. Rolling the wrong way here would push the date LATER and produce
fewer than the required 90 days -- the direction that loses the right. This
is the inverse of every forward rule already seeded, which is precisely why
it needed a real rule and a live proof rather than remaining a code path.
FRCP 6(a)(6) IS DIRECTION-DEPENDENT AND ALREADY IMPLEMENTED, and these rules
are the first seeded data that actually exercises it. State-declared
holidays (kind 'state') count only for periods measured AFTER an event; for
these backward periods the engine correctly ignores them. The federal
calendars loaded in this system carry kind 'federal', which counts in both
directions, so the distinction does not change these particular dates -- but
the code path is now reachable from real data rather than tests alone.
NOT SEEDED, deliberately: Rule 26(a)(2)(D)(ii)'s 30-day rebuttal disclosure
runs from ANOTHER PARTY'S disclosure rather than from the trial date, so it
is a forward period off a different trigger and does not belong in this file.
Rule 26(a)(3)(B)'s own 14-day objection window likewise runs forward from the
pretrial disclosures. Both are ordinary forward rules and would be added as
such, not bent into this set to inflate it.
ALSO NOTE: all three rules below are expressly subject to a court order or
stipulation setting a different time ('Absent a stipulation or a court
order', 'Unless the court orders otherwise', 'Unless these rules or a court
order provides otherwise'). That condition is quoted in each authority note
so it reaches the audit trail an attorney reads. The engine has no field for
a scheduling order and does not pretend to -- a computed date here is the
RULE'S default, and a scheduling order overrides it.

rules.label: Expert witness disclosures, counted back from the trial date

authority.quote: at least 90 days before the date set for trial or for the case to be ready for trial
authority.note: BACKWARD-counted. Under Rule 6(a)(5) the last day rolls BACKWARD, so a 90th-day landing on a weekend or legal holiday moves to the preceding business day -- rolling forward would yield fewer than the 90 days the rule requires. Trigger name carries the disclosure subject because Rule 26(a)(3)(B) runs backward from the same trial date with a different count; see _readme. Expressly subject to a different time being set: the rule opens 'Absent a stipulation or a court order'. This engine has no field for a scheduling order, so the date below is the rule's default and a scheduling order overrides it.

rules.label: Pretrial disclosures, counted back from the trial date

authority.note: BACKWARD-counted, same Rule 6(a)(5) backward rollover as the expert-disclosure rule. Distinct trigger name from Rule 26(a)(2)(D)(i) on purpose -- both run backward from the trial date, and a shared trigger would place two rules in force at once, which the engine refuses as AMBIGUOUS_RULE rather than picking one. Expressly subject to a different time: 'Unless the court orders otherwise'. The 14-day window for objections to these disclosures runs FORWARD from them and is a separate rule, not seeded here.

rules.label: Service of a written motion and notice of hearing, counted back from the hearing

authority.quote: A written motion and notice of the hearing must be served at least 14 days before the time specified for the hearing
authority.note: BACKWARD-counted from the hearing rather than from a filing, and the only rule in this file whose trigger event is unambiguous on its own, so its trigger name needs no subject qualifier. Expressly subject to exceptions: the rule opens 'Unless these rules or a court order provides otherwise', and 6(c)(1)(A)-(C) carve out ex parte motions and court-set times. No service_extension is attached: Rule 6(d) adds time to a party who must act AFTER BEING SERVED, whereas this period governs the server's own deadline and runs backward from the hearing -- attaching 6(d) here would extend a deadline the rule does not extend, the same distinction already drawn for the waiver rules in the Phase 1 seed.
